questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning of a Living Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: A living constitution is one that is not static but evolves over time through interpretation, amendment, and judicial pronouncements to meet the changing needs of society while preserving its core values.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning of a Living Constitution'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution is described as a living document because it adapts to changing social, political, and economic realities without losing its basic identity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning of a Living Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Introduction: A Living Document

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Amendments and Their Types' refers to.
questions.a: A constitutional amendment is a formal change to the provisions of the Constitution made under Article 368, classified into three types based on the majority required: simple majority, special majority, and special majority plus ratification by half the States.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Amendments and Their Types'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution provides for different amendment procedures depending on the importance of the provision, balancing flexibility with stability.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Amendments and Their Types' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Amendment Procedures

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Basic Structure Doctrine' refers to.
questions.a: The basic structure doctrine is a judicial principle laid down in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) which holds that Parliament cannot, under its amending power, alter or destroy the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Basic Structure Doctrine'.
questions.a: While Parliament has wide amending power under Article 368, it cannot damage or destroy the core features of the Constitution such as democracy, secularism, rule of law, judicial review, and federalism.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Basic Structure Doctrine' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Limits on Amendment: Basic Structure

concepts.title: Judicial Interpretation and the Living Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Judicial Interpretation and the Living Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: Judicial interpretation is the process by which the Supreme Court and High Courts read meaning into constitutional provisions, expanding their scope to address new situations and making the Constitution a living document.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Judicial Interpretation and the Living Constitution'.
questions.a: Through expansive interpretation, the judiciary has expanded rights and adapted the Constitution to changing times, as seen in cases like Maneka Gandhi (1978) which broadened the right to life and personal liberty.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Judicial Interpretation and the Living Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Judicial Interpretation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Flexibility versus Rigidity' refers to.
questions.a: Flexibility allows the Constitution to be amended easily to meet changing needs, while rigidity ensures stability by making amendment difficult; the Indian Constitution combines both features.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Flexibility versus Rigidity'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution is partly rigid and partly flexible, providing enough flexibility to adapt to change and enough rigidity to preserve its essential framework.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Flexibility versus Rigidity' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Balance of Flexibility and Rigidity

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Constitutional Conventions' refers to.
questions.a: Constitutional conventions are unwritten rules and practices that regulate the working of the constitution, filling gaps and guiding institutions even though they are not legally enforceable.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Constitutional Conventions'.
questions.a: Conventions play an important role in the working of the Indian Constitution by guiding conventions of parliamentary government, cabinet responsibility, and the role of constitutional functionaries.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Constitutional Conventions' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Conventions and the Living Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Evolution of the Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The evolution of the Constitution refers to the gradual changes it has undergone through amendments, judicial interpretation, political practices, and conventions since its adoption in 1950.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Evolution of the Constitution'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution has evolved through over a hundred amendments, landmark judicial decisions, and changing political conventions, demonstrating its capacity to grow with the nation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Evolution of the Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Evolution of the Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Future of the Indian Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The future of the Indian Constitution lies in its ability to remain responsive to the aspirations of the people, protect the rights of citizens, and uphold democratic values while adapting to new challenges.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Future of the Indian Constitution'.
questions.a: The Constitution will endure as long as it balances stability with change, protects diversity and unity, and remains committed to the values of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Future of the Indian Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Conclusion: Future of the Constitution
